# Comparing Two Alternatives

This is the single most common pattern in CS empirical work: *"Is system A
faster/better than system B?"*

## Independent Samples: Welch's t-test

When two groups are independent (different runs, different subjects), use
Welch's t-test, which does *not* assume equal variances. It is the default in
R.

```r
set.seed(1)
A <- rnorm(30, mean = 100, sd = 10)
B <- rnorm(30, mean = 105, sd = 14)

t.test(A, B)
```

Output reports:

- `t` statistic and degrees of freedom
- `p-value`
- 95% CI for the *difference of means*

## Paired Data

If the same subjects (or benchmarks, or inputs) are measured under both
conditions, the paired t-test is more powerful because it removes
between-subject variance.

```r
baseline  <- c(120, 95, 200, 60, 150, 180, 75, 110, 130, 95, 210, 88)
optimized <- baseline * runif(12, 0.7, 0.95)

t.test(optimized, baseline, paired = TRUE)
```

A paired design is almost always the right choice when comparing two
algorithms on the same set of benchmarks.

## Effect Size: Cohen's d

The p-value tells you whether an effect exists; the effect size tells you
whether it matters.

```r
library(effsize)
cohen.d(A, B)
```

Conventions: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large. These are rough --- interpret
in your domain.

## Assumptions

The t-test assumes approximate normality of the *sampling distribution of the
mean* (CLT helps for n ≥ ~30) and, for the classical version, equal
variances. Check with diagnostics:

```r
qqnorm(A); qqline(A)
shapiro.test(A)
var.test(A, B)
```

If assumptions fail badly, move to the non-parametric tests in @sec-np.
